newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-WORLD GRAIN GIANTS HIT AT AWB MONOPOLY.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-WORLD GRAIN GIANTS HIT AT AWB MONOPOLY.

text.p: Major international grains trading groups expect substantial investments will be made in the Australian grains industry if the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) and other statutory authorities are stripped of their government monopolies on Australian exports.

Large-scale international grain groups see no reason to undertake substantial investments in grain infrastructure in Australia because of the monopolies of the AWB and the Australian Barley Board (ABB), said John Begg, executive secretary of the Australian Grain Exporters Association.

AGEA members include Cargill Inc, Continental Grain, Louis Dreyfus, Oceania, Joseph, Marubeni, Toepfer and Concordia -- all Australian offshoots of big U.S., European, Japanese and South American grains traders.
Other groups which are not members of the AGEA, such as Japan's Mitsui and Co Ltd, also in recent times have told Reuters that the AWB monopoly is seen as an impediment to private investment.
If the AWB single desk were to go, private investment in grains would be likely to increase strongly, Begg told Reuters in an interview.

"You would see tremendous investment. Companies like the member companies of the AGEA are not investing in the grains business in Australia. Why should they?" he said. He said it was impossible to put a figure on likely investment but it could come from Japan, the European Union and North America, he added. "You would see a very big change," he said.

Under present arrangements, private traders with international wheat buying orders have to ask the AWB for supplies. Under a private system, traders would buy from grains co-operatives and operate their own storage, competing with each other for farmers produce.
"We wouldn't have to go cap in hand to the Wheat Board and say 'please give me something', only to have the Wheat Board say 'look, I've got this reserved, you can't have it," Begg said.
It was impossible to estimate how much of the market the private trade would take if the AWB export monopoly were removed, Begg said.
He said major international grains traders were unable to assess whether the AWB and ABB will retain export monopolies, to be reviewed as part of Australian government competition policy.
This was despite declining international fashion for monopoly exporting through statutory authorities, with de-regulation most recently undertaken by Argentina and South Africa, Begg said.

Growing controversy in Canada over the Canadian Wheat Board's monopoly, especially if the Ontario Wheat Board were dissolved as a result of a November vote by farmers, would pressure the federal government through separation arguments from Alberta growers, he added.

This was interesting in view of divisions in the Australian grains industry, primarily between Western Australia and the eastern states, now that Western Australia grower groups were calling for the AWB export monopoly to be split between the west and the east, he said.
"A so-called privatised Wheat Board will, to all intents and purposes, be a private company. So why give the monopoly to one private company and not to another?" Begg said.
"The companies that form our membership have immense ramifications and can bring immense business to Australia."
AGEA would participate in the competition review and hoped for a fair and open debate, he said. "We don't want to see this whole debate screwed up by political pressure," he said.
